unesco.title: Gnawa
unesco.description: Gnawa refers to a set of musical events, performances, fraternal practices and therapeutic rituals mixing the secular with the sacred. Gnawa is first and foremost a Sufi brotherhood music combined with lyrics with a generally religious content, invoking ancestors and spirits. Originally practised by groups and individuals from slavery and the slave trade dating back to at least the 16th century, Gnawa culture is now considered as part of Morocco’s multifaceted culture and identity. The Gnawa, especially in the city, practise a therapeutic possession ritual through all-night rhythm and trance ceremonies combining ancestral African practices, Arab-Muslim influences and native Berber cultural performances. The Gnawa in rural areas organize communal meals offered to marabout saints. Some Gnawa in urban areas use a stringed musical instrument and castanets, while those in rural areas use large drums and castanets. Colourful, embroidered costumes are worn in the city, while white attire with accessories characterize rural practices. The number of fraternal groups and master musicians is constantly growing in Morocco’s villages and major cities, and Gnawa groups – organized into associations – hold local, regional, national and international festivals year-round. This allows young people to learn about both the lyrics and musical instruments as well as practices and rituals related to Gnawa culture generally.

profile.name: Gnawa
profile.tagline: Morocco's UNESCO-listed trance dance driven by iron krakeb castanets and guembri lutes.
profile.insight: During all-night lila ceremonies, master musicians wield the guembri lute and iron krakebs to evoke seven spiritual entities until dawn.
profile.profile: Gnawa is a Moroccan Sufi brotherhood tradition originating from the displacement of West Africans through the trans-Saharan slave trade. Inscribed by UNESCO in 2019, it combines ritual poetry, traditional music, and ecstatic dance within nocturnal healing ceremonies known as lila or derdeba. Guided by a maâlem, practitioners negotiate their relationships with spiritual entities called mluk through hypnotic rhythms.
profile.profile_long:
Gnawa music and dance constitute a vibrant Moroccan tradition rooted in the heritage of enslaved West Africans brought across the Sahara between the 11th and 17th centuries. Peoples from regions spanning Senegal to Chad and Mali to Nigeria established a distinct diasporic identity in Morocco, preserving the memory of historical suffering while integrating deeply into Islamic culture. The tradition is most famously preserved through the lila or derdeba, an all-night communal ceremony dedicated to prayer, healing, and spiritual reintegration. Guided by a maâlem, or master musician, alongside a clairvoyant priestess known as a moqadma or shuwafa, the ritual operates as a complex liturgy that recreates the genesis of the universe through the evocation of seven main spiritual entities or mluk.

The auditory and kinetic foundation of Gnawa relies on a unique configuration of instruments and rhythmic interplay. Central to the ensemble is the hajhuj, guembri, or sentir—a box-shaped, three-stringed lute whose freely vibrating bass string produces a throbbing drone played with a specialized thumb-frailing technique. Accompanying the lute are the qraqab, large and heavy iron castanets that rattle in continuous patterns, and large tbel drums in rural settings. The music is structured around repeating phrases and seven distinct musical suites, each corresponding to a family of mluk characterized by specific colors, incenses, rhythms, and dance steps. As the ceremony progresses through the sacred sequence known as the treq, participants enter a state of ecstatic trance known as jedba, engaging in powerful dances to appease or strengthen bonds with the spiritual entities.

While deeply grounded in sacred Sufi brotherhoods and private healing rites, Gnawa culture has also expanded into public and profane contexts. The annual Gnaoua World Music Festival in Essaouira, launched in 1998, draws hundreds of thousands of visitors, bringing master musicians together with international jazz, blues, reggae, and rock artists for high-energy cross-cultural fusions. Despite these modern adaptations, private lilas continue to safeguard the traditional spiritual framework. In December 2019, Gnawa was officially inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognizing its role in fostering community identity, social cohesion, and the transmission of ancestral heritage across generations in Morocco.

sections.origins_and_history: Gnawa music emerged in Morocco from traditions of enslaved West Africans displaced through the trans-Saharan slave trade between the 11th and 17th centuries. The population originates from a broad region extending from Senegal to Chad and from Mali to Southern Nigeria, maintaining historical links with the royal Black Guard of Morocco.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The ceremony begins with an opening consecration known as the aâda, where musicians perform a swirling acrobatic dance while playing the krakeb castanets. During the lila, participants enter an ecstatic trance state called jedba, performing specialized dances corresponding to the seven families of mluk spirits.
sections.music_and_instruments: Central instruments include the hajhuj (also called guembri or sentir), a three-stringed lute played with a drop-thumb frailing technique, and the qraqab (krakeb), heavy iron castanets. Rural settings also utilize large tbel drums, while melodies emphasize the tonic and fifth with pitch-flattening around the third and seventh degrees.
sections.costume_and_setting: Urban ceremonies feature colourful, embroidered costumes, and dancers are covered by veils of seven different colours corresponding to the specific mluk spirits being invoked. Rural practices are characterized by white attire with specific accessories.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performances occur during lila or derdeba, all-night communal ceremonies of prayer, sacrifice, and healing held from late evening until sunrise. The ritual aims to reintegrate and balance the main powers of the human body through engagement with spiritual entities.
sections.notable_figures: Prominent maâlems include Mahmoud Gania ('the King'), Hamid El Kasri, H'mida Boussou, Chérif Regragui, Allal Soudani, Abdellah El Gourd, and Abdeslam Alikkane, many of whom have bridged traditional rituals with international jazz and world music collaborations.
sections.regional_variants: Maâlems often blend regional styles, such as Gharbaoui from Rabat, Marsaoui from Essaouira, and Soussi or Berber styles from southern Morocco, combining local musical flavors into their repertoire.
sections.lineage: Gnawa maintains spiritual and musical ties to West African traditions such as the Hausa halam lute, while existing as a distinct Moroccan Sufi brotherhood tradition recognized by UNESCO.

profile.sacred_note: Gnawa features sacred possession rituals (jedba and lila) involving spiritual entities (mluk) and animal sacrifice; outsiders must respect the spiritual boundaries of these healing ceremonies.

activation_questions.question: How do distinct regional Moroccan variants (such as Marsaoui from Essaouira, Gharbaoui from Rabat, and Marrakchi) differentiate their movement vocabularies during the lila?
activation_questions.why_needed: Sources note different stylistic origins of maâlems but lack granular breakdowns of specific footwork or body configurations per region.
activation_questions.next_evidence: Field recordings and anthropological studies documenting local zriba spatial configurations and step variations.

episode_brief.title_hook: Iron Castanets and the Night of Trance
episode_brief.logline: Explore the UNESCO-listed Gnawa tradition of Morocco through its hypnotic lila ceremonies, master musicians, and ancestral West African roots.
beats: A 19th-century slave heritage rooted in West Africa and integrated into Moroccan Islamic culture.
The maâlem tuning the box-shaped guembri lute as incense burns in the evening air.
The metallic clatter of qraqab iron castanets opening the lila ceremony.
The swirling acrobatic movements of the aâda consecration.
The ecstatic jedba trance dance invoking the seven families of mluk spirits until dawn.
